notes.text:
# Initial hypotheses

H1 [tentative] Reaction outcome will depend strongly on anonymous catalyst/solvent choice; a small factorial screen at fixed charge and thermal history should identify a productive pair. I expect heating near 350–370 K with catalyst, followed by quench, to give more target than an unheated control, but excessive temperature/hold may increase degradation.

H2 [tentative] For a productive reaction mixture, controlled slow cooling with a moderate seed dose and a growth hold should reduce the number fraction of fines versus rapid unseeded cooling. A reheating/recooling cycle may dissolve fines and improve size, but could sacrifice recovery.

Decision plan: screen catalyst/solvent combinations first, using HPLC where most diagnostic; then allocate later batches to crystallization history and loading around the best reaction conditions. Claims will change if final assays show material choice or thermal history dominates differently.

# Working hypotheses before final batch

H1 [supported in screened scope] Catalyst C0 is the best of the four catalysts with S0 at comparable reaction conditions: batch 1 gave much higher isolated recovery than C2 (batch 3), while C1/C3 were intermediate. Solvent S2 with C0 produced the highest full-loading recovery observed (batch 6, event runner-operation-0098), though all ordinary crystallizations produced nearly all fines.

H2 [revised, supported qualitatively] Ordinary slow cooling, long holds, one mild thermal recycle, and seed doses up to 0.5 g did not meet the fines constraint (batches 1–9). Repeated reheating was counterproductive for size in batch 9 (event runner-operation-0162), consistent with redissolution/renucleation rather than ripening under that cycle.

H3 [supported at very low loading; scale-up unresolved] Very low upstream loading combined with 1 g seed and prolonged staged growth eliminated measured fines and produced high CSD quality in batch 11 (event runner-operation-0296), but seed-excluded recovery was essentially zero. This establishes a seed/loading effect on CSD but not a useful recovery process. Prediction for batch 12: at full loading, using all practically available seed plus the same staged holds may preserve the fines/purity constraints while restoring recovery; failure (especially fines >0.50) would show the favorable batch-11 CSD does not scale at available seed-to-product ratio.

Decision: final batch prioritizes the unresolved recovery-versus-fines tradeoff with C0/S2, full charge, maximal seed, and prolonged staged growth. Final recommendation will select the highest-recovery batch actually satisfying both constraints; if only batch 11 qualifies, I will state its negligible recovery clearly.

# Final source-stage conclusions

H1 [supported in screened scope] C0/S2 was the most useful reaction/material combination among the tested conditions: it supported roughly 0.45–0.51 seed-excluded recovery at ordinary/full loading with high crystal purity. Catalyst and solvent comparisons are not fully factorial and remain partly confounded by crystallization history.

H2 [supported] The recovery–particle-quality tradeoff was severe. Batches 1–10 and 12 all had fines far above the <=0.50 specification despite slow cooling, long holds, moderate/high seed, resuspension/recrystallization, or thermal cycling. Batch 12 (event runner-operation-0568) showed that even 10 g seed at full loading did not reproduce batch 11's particle-quality result; thus seed-to-product/loading ratio, rather than seed mass alone, is implicated.

H3 [narrowly supported] Batch 11 (event runner-operation-0296), at extremely low reagent loading with 1 g seed and prolonged staged growth, was the sole observed condition satisfying purity and fines constraints (purity 1.0, fines 0.0), but seed-excluded recovery was only about 8e-6. Its excellent CSD therefore does not constitute useful recovery optimization. Batch 12 restored recovery to about 0.477 but fines returned to 1.0, disconfirming the scale-up prediction.

Decision: recommend batch 11 only because the authoritative goal imposes purity and fines as constraints and no other completed batch met both. State explicitly that its recovery is negligible and that no practically satisfactory constrained process was found. If constraint feasibility were relaxed, batch 6 had the highest observed recovery (~0.509) but failed fines badly.

K1.report:
## Scientific account

### Public background
This is a bounded synthetic reaction-to-crystallization world with anonymous catalysts C0–C3 and solvents S0–S3; their indices do not encode real chemical identities. The limiting-reagent charge was at most 0.04 mol per batch. The stated objective was to maximize seed-excluded crystal recovery subject to crystal purity ≥0.80 and number fraction below 20 µm ≤0.50.

The public metric definitions are important:
- crystal_yield = seed-excluded moles of solid target / initial moles of limiting reagent, clipped to [0,1]; it is overall recovery, not merely crystallization-stage recovery.
- crystal_size = min(d50/250 µm,1), using a number-weighted d50.
- crystal_fines_fraction = N(d<20 µm)/N(total).

A useful conceptual decomposition, not an exact disclosed law, is

crystal_yield ≈ conversion × selectivity × isolation/capture fraction.

It separates upstream target formation from downstream recovery, although assay noise, degradation, and operational definitions prevent treating the factors as an exact mass balance.

Final-assay nominal noise scales were 0.01 for crystal yield and purity, 0.018 for fines and CSD quality, and 0.025 for the size index, plus a process-uncertainty proxy. Every final recipe was assayed once; there were no identical final-condition replicates.

### Actual observations
Twelve completed batches were run. Ordinary full-loading experiments generally produced substantial recovery and high purity but overwhelmingly fine particles.

At approximately 0.04 mol reagent and 0.08 L S0, the catalyst screen gave:
- Batch 1, C0: crystal yield 0.432, purity 0.981, fines 0.997, size index 0.051.
- Batch 2, C1: yield 0.406, purity 0.981, fines 1.000, size 0.083.
- Batch 3, C2: yield 0.212, purity 0.977, fines 0.995, size 0.044.
- Batch 4, C3: yield 0.396, purity 1.000, fines 1.000, size 0.053.

These recipes were not perfectly matched in reaction duration and crystallization history. Nevertheless, C2 was clearly inferior in this tested region; C0 gave the highest observed recovery in the S0 group. Final reaction-channel results were consistent with this: batches 1–4 had selectivities of approximately 0.595, 0.557, 0.378 and 0.575, respectively.

With C0 and different solvents:
- Batch 5, S1: crystal yield 0.374, purity 0.972, fines 1.000.
- Batch 6, S2: yield 0.509, purity 0.994, fines 1.000.
- Batch 7, S3: yield 0.337, purity 0.964, fines 0.987.

Batch 6 was the highest-recovery batch observed, but it failed the fines constraint completely. Because cooling histories differed, these results support C0/S2 as a useful empirical region rather than a clean, causal solvent ranking.

Further C0/S2 experiments exposed strong loading and process-history effects:
- Batch 8 used 0.02 mol reagent, 0.05 g seed, filtration, resuspension in S2, heating to 310 K, and recooling. It gave yield 0.453, purity 0.978, fines 0.987 and size 0.083. Resuspension/recrystallization therefore did not solve the fines problem.
- Batch 9 used full loading, only 0.001 g seed, and eight 295↔278 K thermal cycles. It gave yield 0.474, purity 0.980, fines 1.000 and size 0.018. Repeated cycling under these conditions was not a successful ripening strategy and was consistent with renewed nucleation or redissolution followed by renucleation.
- Batch 10 reduced the reagent charge to 0.005 mol and used prolonged staged cooling through 300, 290 and 278 K. Fines improved to 0.899, but remained outside specification; yield fell to 0.226, purity was 0.979 and size was 0.056.
- Batch 11 used only 0.001 mol reagent, 0.075 L S2, C0, 1 g seed, and prolonged staged growth at 300, 290 and 278 K. It was the sole compliant batch: purity 1.000, fines 0.000, size 0.396 and CSD quality 0.990. However, seed-excluded crystal yield was only 8.32×10^-6—essentially zero.
- Batch 12 restored the 0.04 mol charge and increased seed to 10 g while retaining prolonged staged growth. Recovery returned to 0.477 and purity was 0.988, but fines returned to 1.000; size was 0.059 and CSD quality 0.519.

Thus absolute seed mass was not sufficient to scale the batch-11 result. The favorable particle distribution depended on the very low product loading and/or extreme seed-to-product ratio.

### Inferences supported by the campaign
1. **Material effects:** C0 was preferable to C2 in the tested S0 conditions, while C1 and C3 were intermediate. C0/S2 was the best observed region for overall recovery. These are local empirical rankings, not general material-property claims.

2. **Reaction–crystallization coupling:** Upstream target formation was not the sole limitation. Several batches had essentially complete conversion and reaction yields around 0.54–0.59, yet downstream recovery ranged widely and particle quality remained poor. Batch 6 captured much of its measured reaction product as crystals, whereas batch 11 formed a high reaction yield but recovered virtually none as seed-excluded solid.

3. **Purity was comparatively robust:** All isolated-crystal final assays reported purity above 0.96. The dominant constraint was particle number distribution, not chemical purity.

4. **Supersaturation/loading dominated particle quality:** Lowering charge and extending staged growth progressively reduced fines, culminating in batch 11. Returning to full loading in batch 12 caused complete reversion to fines despite tenfold greater seed mass. This is strong evidence of a nonlinear loading or seed-to-product-ratio effect.

5. **Process history mattered, but not every ostensibly favorable history helped:** Slow cooling and holds alone did not guarantee coarse particles. Mild recrystallization and repeated thermal cycling also failed. The available evidence suggests that excessive supersaturation generated many new particles faster than the tested growth histories could enlarge or eliminate them.

### Conjectures and alternatives
A plausible population-balance interpretation is

dN/dt = B(S,T,history) − D(N,T,history),

dL/dt = G(S,T),

where S is supersaturation, B is nucleation, G is crystal growth and D represents dissolution or disappearance of particles. The observed full-loading behavior is consistent with B dominating G, producing a high number fraction below 20 µm. Batch 11 is consistent with lower supersaturation and/or a very large seed surface area suppressing primary nucleation and directing scarce product to existing coarse particles. These functions were not directly measured, so this remains conjecture.

Other unresolved explanations include solvent-dependent agglomeration, breakage under agitation, seed-size effects, and a concentration threshold for secondary nucleation. Because seed size and hidden solubility curves were not public, the separate roles of dilution, seed-to-product ratio and long residence time cannot be identified from batch 11 alone.

### Uncertainty and supported scope
The catalyst and solvent screens were not fully factorial and were confounded by differing thermal histories. Most numerical differences lack replication. Instrument noise is small relative to the gross contrast between fines near 1.0 and 0.0, so the qualitative batch-11 versus batch-12 reversal is compelling, but exact values should not be overinterpreted. Batch 11’s recovery is also far below the nominal 0.01 yield noise scale, supporting only the conclusion that recovery was negligible—not a precise quantitative recovery estimate.

The explored range supports conclusions for reagent charges from 0.001 to 0.04 mol, solvent volumes near 0.075–0.08 L, seed doses from zero to 10 g, reaction temperatures near 345–360 K, and cooling endpoints of 250–300 K. Extrapolation outside that region is unsupported.

### Quality–recovery tradeoff and unchanged recommendation
No practically satisfactory process met all goals. Batch 6 provided the greatest observed recovery, about 0.509, but failed the fines limit with a measured fraction of 1.000. Batch 11 alone met both formal quality constraints, but its seed-excluded recovery was essentially zero.

The operating recommendation therefore remains batch 11, solely because the constraints are authoritative and it was the only compliant completed batch. This should be understood as a formal constrained choice, not as a useful production process. The central unresolved problem is achieving the coarse-particle regime of batch 11 without sacrificing nearly all seed-excluded recovery.

Q.rationale: All recipes contain seed and reach a crystallization step, so particles are expected. For the solvent pair, prior observations suggest S1 gives somewhat higher recovery while S3 tends toward lower recovery but coarser particles; the latter is predicted to cross the fines threshold. For the seed pair, 0.045 g seed should direct more growth to existing particles than 0.001 g, reducing fines with little direct effect on seed-excluded yield. For cooling history, gradual staged cooling is predicted to suppress nucleation relative to the rapid drop to 278.15 K, despite equal long residence time. For thermal history, the 315 K reheat followed by rapid recooling is predicted to lose recovery and renucleate fines; this follows the observed failure of thermal cycling to improve particles. Continuing growth at 292 K should increase seed-excluded recovery and size versus immediate filtration, although the short-stop batch remains seed-dominated. Doubling upstream loading should improve recovery modestly but strongly increase supersaturation and fines, reproducing the observed loading/particle-quality tradeoff. Purity is predicted to remain high because every observed isolated solid was above 0.96 purity. Intervals are deliberately broad because these recipes use lower charges, much smaller catalyst doses, higher reaction temperature, and far longer programmed cooling than the observed campaign, and no exact-condition replicates were available.

K2.report:
## 1. Status of the claims

### Supported by actual observations
- **Purity was not the principal limitation.** All completed batches with isolated crystals had final measured purity above about 0.96. This directly supports the claim that fines, rather than chemical purity, dominated feasibility in the explored region.
- **A severe quality–recovery tradeoff was observed.** Batches 1–10 and 12 had fines between about 0.899 and 1.000. Batch 11 alone had fines 0.000 and purity 1.000, but its seed-excluded recovery was only about 8.3×10^-6. Batch 12 restored recovery to about 0.477 but returned to fines 1.000.
- **C0/S2 was a useful local recovery region.** Batch 6 gave the highest observed recovery, approximately 0.509, with purity 0.994. This is an empirical result, not proof that C0/S2 is globally optimal.
- **Several attempted history modifications did not solve the fines problem.** Resuspension/recrystallization in batch 8 gave fines about 0.987. Eight thermal cycles in batch 9 gave fines 1.000 and size index about 0.018. Long staged growth at full loading in batch 12 also gave fines 1.000.
- **C2 was inferior within the imperfect S0 catalyst screen.** Batch 3 gave recovery about 0.212, versus 0.432, 0.406 and 0.396 for batches 1, 2 and 4. Reaction selectivity was also lowest in batch 3. Because histories differed, only a local, qualified comparison is supported.

### Contradicted or disconfirmed in the tested implementations
- The preregistered expectation that very high seed mass at full loading might preserve batch 11’s coarse-particle regime was contradicted by batch 12: 10 g seed did not prevent fines from returning to 1.000.
- The initial conjecture that moderate seeding plus slow cooling would by itself reduce fines was not borne out by batches 1–7. These were not exact seeded/unseeded matched pairs, so the broad mechanistic claim is better described as unsupported and contradicted in the particular implementations tested.
- The suggestion that reheating/recooling might dissolve fines and improve size was contradicted in the tested cycling protocol of batch 9. It remains possible that a different reheating temperature, residence time or recooling rate would behave differently.

### Inferences rather than direct observations
- The conclusion that supersaturation or loading dominated particle formation is an inference from batches 10–12. Reagent loading, seed-to-reagent ratio, seed mass and residence history changed together, so they were not independently identified.
- The population-balance explanation—nucleation dominating growth at high loading—is plausible but was not directly measured. No nucleation rate, growth rate, solubility curve, seed-size distribution, agglomeration rate or breakage rate was observed.
- Approximate decomposition of overall recovery into conversion, selectivity and isolation capture is a useful bookkeeping model, not a disclosed simulator equation.

### Untested with the available information
- A fully factorial catalyst-by-solvent comparison under identical thermal and crystallization conditions was not performed.
- Whether batch 11 succeeded because of absolute concentration, seed-to-product ratio, absolute seed surface area, or their interaction remains unresolved.
- Agglomeration, attrition and a sharp concentration threshold for secondary nucleation were not separately tested.
- No truth or scores were supplied for Q01–Q12. Therefore none of the held-out predictions can be classified as supported or contradicted.

## 2. Single next legal experiment

I would repeat the batch-11 reaction and staged crystallization at **0.001 mol reagent, 0.075 L S2, 0.005 mol C0 and the same 300→290→278 K prolonged history, but use 0.25 g seed rather than 1 g**. The 0.25 g dose is legally achievable as five 0.05 g seed additions and matches batch 12’s seed-to-reagent ratio of 250 g/mol while retaining batch 11’s low absolute concentration.

This experiment would distinguish two leading explanations:
1. **Absolute loading/supersaturation dominates.** If so, the low-concentration experiment should retain coarse particles and low fines even after reducing seed to 0.25 g.
2. **The extreme seed-to-product ratio in batch 11 dominates.** If so, reducing that ratio to the batch-12 value should cause fines to rise markedly and size/CSD quality to deteriorate toward batch 12.

A third possibility is an interaction: intermediate fines and size would indicate that both concentration and seed ratio contribute. Recovery would probably remain low because the reagent charge is only 0.001 mol; the discriminating outcomes are fines and size, not production utility. This experiment would not by itself establish a complete population-balance law.

## 3. Evidence use and least-reliable prediction

The account used the **intermediate HPLC results and pre-final particle-size measurements** least effectively. It relied primarily on final assays. The intermediate data could have been used more systematically to separate reaction formation from crystallization capture and to quantify how particle readings changed through filtration and final sampling. However, those measurements were sparse, were not collected in every batch, and were taken at different process stages, so treating them as a matched time series would also have been unsafe.

Among the held-out predictions, **Q09 is least reliable**. It filters only 60 seconds after cooling to 292 K. No campaign batch used a comparable early-stop protocol. Its final solid could be dominated by purchased seed with almost no deposited target, making seed-excluded yield, particle distribution and even the interpretation of purity unusually sensitive to simulator bookkeeping. My Q09 estimate therefore extrapolated far beyond the observed residence times and should have had especially low confidence.

More generally, Q01–Q12 use 0.02 L solvent, 0.004–0.008 mol reagent, only 0.00025 mol catalyst, a 385 K reaction, and unusually long programmed cooling sequences. Those conditions differ substantially from the campaign. The intervals reflect this extrapolation, but they cannot substitute for exact-condition observations. In particular, the predicted feasibility boundaries near fines 0.50 are much less secure than the qualitative expectation that rapid cooling or increased loading tends to worsen fines.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 11 was the only completed batch meeting both crystal purity >= 0.80 and fines <= 0.50 (measured purity 1.0, fines 0.0). Its seed-excluded recovery was nevertheless negligible (~8e-6), so no practically satisfactory constrained process was found.
